claims.text: The Open/Closed Principle: software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification.
claims.source_hint: glossary entry ocp; standard formulation in software design literature

claims.text: ShippingFeeIfElseChain.ForOrder(string kind, int totalVnd) returns 0/30,000 for "standard" (threshold 2,000,000), 60,000 for "express", 0 for "pickup", and throws ArgumentException("unknown shipping kind: {kind}") otherwise.

ShippingFee is an abstract class with abstract int ForOrder(int totalVnd); StandardShipping (0 from 2,000,000, else 30,000), ExpressShipping (60,000) and PickUpInStore (0) are sealed classes overriding it — the same fees as the chain.
In C#, a non-abstract class deriving from an abstract class that does not override every abstract member fails to compile (CS0534).

At stage-1, SamplesTests.cs has ShippingFeeTests checking StandardShipping at 1,999,999 and 2,000,000 and all three kinds via ForOrder(2_000_000); adding a new subclass requires no edit to these tests to keep them passing.

Code that only calls ForOrder through a ShippingFee variable does not change when a new subclass is added; some code still has to create an instance of the new class, possibly by editing where the kind is chosen.
ShippingFeeIfElseChain.ForOrder("same_day", 500_000) throws ArgumentException with message "unknown shipping kind: same_day"; supporting it means adding a branch inside ForOrder.

claims.text: OCP concerns adding new cases; changing how an existing case behaves (e.g. the standard free-shipping threshold) is still an edit to that case's class and does not violate OCP.
claims.source_hint: outline misconception 1; common reading of OCP

claims.text: An abstract class or interface does not by itself give OCP: if callers check which concrete class they have, each new kind still requires editing those checks.
claims.source_hint: outline misconception 2; follows from the OCP definition
